ideas.name: Institutional reward structures quietly push researchers off integrity
ideas.statement: People under pressure to keep funding, status, or a program running will tend to shade their research and reporting toward whatever sustains that support, even without intending to be dishonest.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: The examples of the cosmologist, the senator's advice, and the accelerator lab only add up to a warning if the reader already supplies the general mechanism that institutional incentives bend behavior; the piece just lists instances without arguing why they happen.

occurrences.quote: “Yes, but then we won’t get support for more research of this kind.”
occurrences.reasoning: This justification only reads as a corruption of integrity if the reader assumes funding pressure systematically distorts honest communication.

occurrences.quote: they are destroying—possibly—the value of the experiments themselves, which is the whole purpose of the thing
occurrences.reasoning: Only makes sense as a general warning if institutional pressure for publishable results is assumed to routinely override scientific care, which the passage asserts but does not establish.

ideas.name: Cargo cult science: right form, missing substance
ideas.statement: An activity can copy every outward form and procedure of science while lacking the one thing that makes science actually work, so it produces no real results despite looking exactly right.

occurrences.quote: They’re doing everything right. The form is perfect. It looks exactly the way it looked before. But it doesn’t work. No airplanes land.
occurrences.reasoning: States the core metaphor and names the condition directly.

occurrences.quote: That is the idea that we all hope you have learned in studying science in school—we never explicitly say what this is, but just hope that you catch on by all the examples of scientific investigation.
occurrences.reasoning: Explains that the missing ingredient is usually left implicit, which is why the cargo cult can persist unnoticed.

occurrences.quote: That’s why the planes don’t land—but they don’t land.
occurrences.reasoning: Reaffirms that the diagnostic sign of cargo cult science is simply failure to produce working results.

ideas.name: Integrity as deliberately reporting what could prove you wrong
ideas.statement: Real scientific honesty is not merely avoiding false statements; it requires actively volunteering every fact, alternative explanation, and failed check that might undermine your own conclusion.

occurrences.quote: a kind of scientific integrity, a principle of scientific thought that corresponds to a kind of utter honesty—a kind of leaning over backwards
occurrences.reasoning: Defines integrity as going beyond truth-telling into active self-undermining disclosure.

occurrences.quote: Details that could throw doubt on your interpretation must be given, if you know them.
occurrences.reasoning: Spells out the obligation to surface disconfirming detail, not just accurate detail.

occurrences.quote: it’s a matter of scientific integrity, which is another level. The fact that should be added to that advertising statement is that no oils soak through food, if operated at a certain temperature.
occurrences.reasoning: Shows the gap between being technically true and being fully forthcoming about what the claim implies.

ideas.name: You are your own easiest mark
ideas.statement: The primary danger in research is deceiving yourself, not deceiving others; guarding against self-deception has to come first because it is harder to detect than guarding against lying to others.

occurrences.quote: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself—and you are the easiest person to fool.
occurrences.reasoning: States the idea directly as the foundational principle.

occurrences.quote: Millikan measured the charge on an electron by an experiment with falling oil drops and got an answer which we now know not to be quite right.
occurrences.reasoning: Sets up the case study that illustrates unconscious self-deception rather than deliberate fraud.

occurrences.quote: When they got a number that was too high above Millikan’s, they thought something must be wrong—and they would look for and find a reason why something might be wrong.
occurrences.reasoning: Shows researchers unknowingly fooling themselves by trusting an authority's prior result over their own data.

ideas.name: A result only counts once you find what the subject is really responding to
ideas.statement: A behavior isn't properly explained by the variable you intended to manipulate until you've ruled out every other cue the subject could be using instead, however unlikely each seems.

occurrences.quote: Obviously there was something about the door that was different from the other doors.
occurrences.reasoning: Frames the problem as needing to locate the true causal cue rather than assume the intended one.

occurrences.quote: He finally found that they could tell by the way the floor sounded when they ran over it.
occurrences.reasoning: Shows the eventual discovery of the actual operative cue after systematically eliminating others.
